opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That question is really what got me into research in the first place, through the lottery ticket hypothesis. Jonathan Frankle and Michael Carbin showed that inside a large, randomly initialized network there are sparse subnetworks that, if you rewind them to their original initialization and train them alone, can match the full network's accuracy. That raised the question: what is special about those particular weights?

In our "Deconstructing Lottery Tickets" work, we looked at a few pieces of the procedure. One was the masking criterion. Frankle and Carbin kept the weights with the largest final magnitude, but we tried other criteria, such as keeping weights whose magnitude grew the most over training. Those worked well too, which suggested that how a weight *moves* during training, not just where it ends up, tells you something about whether it matters.

Then we looked at what happens to the weights you prune. Setting them to zero turns out to matter. Zero isn't a neutral choice: the pruned weights were often already heading toward zero during training, so freezing them there is in some sense consistent with where optimization was taking them. If you freeze them at their initial values instead, things work much worse.

Signs turned out to matter a lot too. If you keep the mask and the sign of each weight's initial value but reinitialize the magnitudes, the subnetwork still trains well. If you scramble the signs, it falls apart. So a lot of the useful information seems to be in which direction each weight starts out pointing relative to where training wants it to go.

That led to the most surprising result, which we called supermasks. If you apply the lottery-ticket mask to the untrained, randomly initialized network, with no training at all, you get accuracy well above chance. On MNIST it was quite high. We then learned masks directly, optimizing only which weights to keep while the weights stayed at their random values, and those performed even better. So the act of choosing which weights to zero out is itself a form of training.

The general lesson for me was that a weight's trajectory, its sign, and whether it is growing or shrinking carry a lot of structure, and that pruning and training are more closely intertwined than they first appear. That view also shaped my later work on forgetting. If you selectively reset or perturb parts of a network during training, and do it in the right way, the network can end up learning more generalizable features rather than simply losing information. The dynamics of individual weights turn out to be a useful lens for understanding what a network is actually learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I understand it much less well than I'd like, and that discomfort is sort of what drove a lot of my early work.

The thing that got me started was the lottery ticket hypothesis from Jonathan Frankle and Michael Carbin. The claim was that inside a big randomly initialized network there's a small subnetwork that, if you train it alone from the same initialization, matches the full network. That result raised an obvious question for me: what is it about those specific weights and those specific initial values that matters? So in "Deconstructing Lottery Tickets" we just started pulling the procedure apart piece by piece.

A few things fell out that changed how I think about individual weights. First, the exact initial values turned out not to be the important part. What mattered was the sign. If you kept the sign of each winning-ticket weight and reset the magnitudes to something arbitrary, training still worked. Flip the signs and it fell apart. So a lot of what we call "a good initialization" might really be "a good sign pattern."

Second, the pruning criterion that works, keeping large-magnitude weights, can be reinterpreted as keeping weights that moved away from zero during training. Weights that got pushed toward zero are the ones you can drop. That's a statement about trajectories, not just endpoints. Each weight has a little history, and the history tells you whether it's doing work.

The third thing was the one that surprised me most. We found what we called supermasks. You take a randomly initialized network, don't train the weights at all, and just choose which ones to keep. With the right mask you get well above chance accuracy, sometimes quite high, on things like MNIST and CIFAR. That suggests the random weights already contain a lot of usable structure, and training is partly a process of selection rather than purely one of synthesis.

So where does that leave me on how weights evolve? My working picture is that gradient descent is doing something coarser than we usually imagine. Instead of carefully sculpting each parameter to a precise value, it's largely deciding, for each weight, "keep you, pointing this way, and grow you" or "you're noise, shrink." The fine-grained values look less fundamental than the discrete-ish decisions underneath. That's a hypothesis, not a theorem, and there are plenty of settings, especially at scale and with pretraining, where I think the story is richer than that.

What I try to hold onto from that work is more methodological than any single finding. Networks are built out of millions of tiny, individually inscrutable numbers, and the temptation is to reason about them only in aggregate. But some of the most informative experiments are ones where you intervene at the level of individual weights, freeze them, rewind them, flip them, and see what breaks. You learn more from an ablation that fails in an interesting way than from a loss curve that goes down.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the value of a weight from the role it plays in the network. During training, each weight is updated according to how changing it would affect the loss. But that depends on all the other weights, which are changing too. So an individual weight’s trajectory is part of a coupled process, rather than an independent search for the right value.

That also makes trajectories difficult to interpret. A weight might change very little while the computation it participates in changes substantially. Or it might change a lot without a corresponding change in the network’s behavior. So I’d want to look at individual weights alongside changes in representations and predictions, rather than treat their movement as a direct measure of what the network has learned.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think of a weight less as an isolated number and more as part of a system. Its update depends on the examples the network sees, the gradients those examples produce, and what all the other weights are doing. So the same numerical change can mean very different things at different points in training.

One useful question is how much the initial value determines where a weight ends up. Does it preserve its sign or its relative magnitude? Can it move substantially while the network’s overall behavior stays similar? Those give you different views of what learning is doing.

But I’d be cautious about assigning a particular meaning to one weight’s trajectory. Neural networks have a lot of redundancy, and their representations are distributed. Looking at patterns across weights—and connecting those patterns to changes in the network’s behavior—is usually more informative than following a single number.
